nameStory: The Common Pink Flat-back gets its name from its surprisingly rosy coloration and distinctive flattened body shape. Unlike the cylindrical millipedes most people picture, these creatures have broad, flat backs that make them look like tiny armored tanks crawling through the leaf litter.
description: The Common Pink Flat-back is a small millipede that looks quite different from the typical "worm-like" millipedes most people know. Instead of being round, its body is notably flattened and segmented, with each segment bearing two pairs of legs. These millipedes are typically pinkish to salmon-colored and grow to about half an inch to an inch long. They're gentle decomposers that help break down dead plant material in the forest floor.

idTips.label: Flattened body shape
idTips.description: The body is distinctly flat rather than cylindrical, feeling almost like a tiny flexible ruler when gently handled

idTips.label: Pink to salmon coloration
idTips.description: Body ranges from pale pink to deeper salmon or reddish hues, sometimes with slightly darker edges on each segment

idTips.label: Segmented appearance
idTips.description: Body clearly divided into distinct segments, each with small projections called paranota that stick out slightly from the sides

idTips.label: Two pairs of legs per segment
idTips.description: Each body segment has four tiny legs that create a wave-like motion when the millipede walks

idTips.label: Size and movement
idTips.description: About the length of a paperclip, moves slowly and deliberately, often curling into a loose spiral when disturbed

habitat: Look for Common Pink Flat-backs in moist deciduous and mixed forests throughout New England, particularly under rotting logs, leaf litter, and decomposing wood. They prefer areas with rich, dark soil and high humidity levels. You'll often find them in the same spots where you might discover salamanders or other moisture-loving creatures.

seasonality.spring: Active as soil warms and becomes workable, often found under logs and stones as snow melts. This is when they're easiest to spot as they emerge from deeper winter hideouts.
seasonality.summer: Most active during humid periods, especially after rain. Look under bark and in rotting wood where moisture levels stay consistent.
seasonality.fall: Very active as they feed on freshly fallen leaves. Often found in deeper leaf litter as they prepare for winter dormancy.
seasonality.winter: Dormant and hidden deep in soil, under logs, or in other protected spots. Rarely seen unless you dig into their winter shelters.

funFact: Despite being called millipedes (meaning "thousand feet"), Common Pink Flat-backs typically have fewer than 100 legs total, and they're born with just three pairs of legs, growing more segments and legs each time they molt throughout their lives!
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with other small flat-backed millipedes, but the pink coloration is distinctive. Remember: if it's flat and pink, you've probably found your Pink Flat-back. Centipedes move much faster and have only one pair of legs per segment.
contextualKnowledge: The name "millipede" literally means "thousand feet," but this is a huge exaggeration - no millipede actually has anywhere close to 1,000 legs. This naming confusion dates back to ancient times when people simply saw lots of legs and assumed there must be thousands.
compareHints: The Common Pink Flat-back is distinguished from its close relative, the Canadian Flat-back Millipede, primarily by its consistent pink coloration and slightly smaller size. Canadian Flat-backs tend to be more variable in color, often appearing brownish or grayish rather than the distinctive salmon-pink of this species.

relatedSpecies.distinction: The Canadian Flat-back is easily separated from its close relative, the Common Pink Flat-back Millipede, by that distinctive black mid-dorsal stripe running down its back.
